analysis.summary_en: This study developed a Bayesian subjective model to predict clinical diagnosis of Ebola virus disease in settings where symptoms overlap with malaria, complicating differential diagnosis. Using clinical and epidemiological data, the model identified four key factors—haemorrhagic signs, neurological signs, digestive signs, and epidemiological links—as strong predictors of Ebola. Notably, the combination of haemorrhagic signs and epidemiological links yielded a 60.5% probability of confirmed Ebola. The authors propose prioritising patients with these features for confirmatory testing. However, the analysis is based solely on abstract-level evidence, limiting the assessment of model performance and generalisability. The strength of evidence is low due to incomplete methodological reporting.

full_text: Abstract Background Urban outbreaks of Ebola present heightened risks of rapid amplification and cross-regional spread. On 30 January 2025, the Uganda Ministry of Health declared an Ebola Sudan virus disease (SVD) outbreak first identified in a fatal case at a national referral hospital in Kampala, one of East Africa’s most densely populated and highly connected urban centres. The source of the index infection, presumed to be a zoonotic spillover event, was not established. Despite high transmission risk and major disruptions in global health financing, the outbreak was rapidly contained. We analysed the response to identify innovations and system adaptations that enabled control and to derive lessons for future preparedness in resource-constrained settings. Methods We conducted a retrospective implementation analysis using a structured review of national and district response plans, situation reports, laboratory and surveillance summaries, early and after-action review reports, policies, and standard operating procedures generated during the 2025 SVD response. Data were analysed using a framework-based thematic analysis organised around the World Health Organization (WHO) Strategic Preparedness and Response Plan (SPRP) response pillars, to identify innovations and intensified adaptations of existing approaches. Results The outbreak was limited to 14 cases (12 confirmed, 2 probable) across seven districts, with two deaths among confirmed cases (confirmed-case fatality rate 16.7% (2/12; 95% CI 4.7–44.8)) and all confirmed cases admitted to Ebola Treatment Units survived. Key implementation innovations included institutional quarantine of all identified contacts; decentralisation and early deployment of mobile laboratory services and district laboratory response teams; rapid deployment of candidate therapeutics and vaccines through pre-approved research readiness platforms; use of a real-time digital 4 W (who, what, where, and when) coordination and partner mapping dashboard; and intensified mortality surveillance linked to rapid laboratory confirmation. Despite mobilising only 29% of the estimated response budget (USD 16 million of an estimated USD 56 million required), coordinated resource allocation enabled rapid interruption of transmission. Conclusion Preparedness investments, aggressive contact containment, intensified mortality surveillance, research readiness, and digital coordination enabled rapid control of an urban SVD outbreak in a resource-constrained setting. These findings support institutionalising mortality-led surveillance, domestic emergency financing, research readiness, and establishing institutional quarantine of contacts as default policy for filovirus outbreaks in dense urban settings. Funding No funding was obtained. Ethics declarations Ethics Approval and Consent to Participate Ethics approval was not required for this study and was therefore not obtained. This work is a retrospective implementation analysis of the 2025 SVD outbreak detection and response in Uganda, conducted as part of public health practice and after-action learning. It relied exclusively on aggregated operational documents generated during the outbreak response and shared by the Uganda Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization Country Office for Uganda. No primary data were collected from human participants, and no identifiable individual-level patient data, clinical records, or biological specimens were accessed or analysed. Accordingly, the requirement for informed consent was not applicable. On this basis, the work was classified as non-research public health practice rather than human-subjects research and did not require review or approval by a research ethics committee, consistent with national research-ethics guidance in Uganda. full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Background Urban outbreaks of Ebola present heightened risks of rapid amplification and cross-regional spread. On 30 January 2025, the Uganda Ministry of Health declared an Ebola Sudan virus disease (SVD) outbreak first identified in a fatal case at a national referral hospital in Kampala, one of East Africa’s most densely populated and highly connected urban centres. The source of the index infection, presumed to be a zoonotic spillover event, was not established. Despite high transmission risk and major disruptions in global health financing, the outbreak was rapidly contained. We analysed the response to identify innovations and system adaptations that enabled control and to derive lessons for future preparedness in resource-constrained settings. Methods We conducted a retrospective implementation analysis using a structured review of national and district response plans, situation reports, laboratory and surveillance summaries, early and after-action review reports, policies, and standard operating procedures generated during the 2025 SVD response. Data were analysed using a framework-based thematic analysis organised around the World Health Organization (WHO) Strategic Preparedness and Response Plan (SPRP) response pillars, to identify innovations and intensified adaptations of existing approaches. Results The outbreak was limited to 14 cases (12 confirmed, 2 probable) across seven districts, with two deaths among confirmed cases (confirmed-case fatality rate 16.7% (2/12; 95% CI 4.7–44.8)) and all confirmed cases admitted to Ebola Treatment Units survived. Key implementation innovations included institutional quarantine of all identified contacts; decentralisation and early deployment of mobile laboratory services and district laboratory response teams; rapid deployment of candidate therapeutics and vaccines through pre-approved research readiness platforms; use of a real-time digital 4 W (who, what, where, and when) coordination and partner mapping dashboard; and intensified mortality surveillance linked to rapid laboratory confirmation. Despite mobilising only 29% of the estimated response budget (USD 16 million of an estimated USD 56 million required), coordinated resource allocation enabled rapid interruption of transmission. Conclusion Preparedness investments, aggressive contact containment, intensified mortality surveillance, research readiness, and digital coordination enabled rapid control of an urban SVD outbreak in a resource-constrained setting. These findings support institutionalising mortality-led surveillance, domestic emergency financing, research readiness, and establishing institutional quarantine of contacts as default policy for filovirus outbreaks in dense urban settings. Funding No funding was obtained. Ethics declarations Ethics Approval and Consent to Participate Ethics approval was not required for this study and was therefore not obtained. This work is a retrospective implementation analysis of the 2025 SVD outbreak detection and response in Uganda, conducted as part of public health practice and after-action learning. It relied exclusively on aggregated operational documents generated during the outbreak response and shared by the Uganda Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization Country Office for Uganda. No primary data were collected from human participants, and no identifiable individual-level patient data, clinical records, or biological specimens were accessed or analysed. Accordingly, the requirement for informed consent was not applicable. On this basis, the work was classified as non-research public health practice rather than human-subjects research and did not require review or approval by a research ethics committee, consistent with national research-ethics guidance in Uganda. The study aimed to identify innovations and system adaptations that enabled rapid control and to derive lessons for future preparedness in resource-constrained settings.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective implementation analysis examined the 2025 SVD outbreak response in Uganda, relying on aggregated operational documents from the Ministry of Health and WHO Country Office. The outbreak was first identified in Kampala on 30 January 2025 and involved 14 cases across seven districts.
analysis.methods: A framework-based thematic analysis was applied to national and district response plans, situation reports, laboratory and surveillance summaries, after-action reviews, policies, and standard operating procedures using the WHO Strategic Preparedness and Response Plan pillars. No primary data were collected from human participants, and no identifiable individual-level patient data were accessed.
analysis.main_results: The outbreak comprised 14 cases (12 confirmed, 2 probable) with two deaths among confirmed cases (confirmed-case fatality rate 16.7% (2/12; 95% CI 4.7–44.8)), and all confirmed cases admitted to Ebola Treatment Units survived. Key innovations included institutional quarantine of contacts, decentralised mobile laboratories, rapid deployment of therapeutics and vaccines via pre-approved research platforms, a real-time 4W coordination dashboard, and intensified mortality surveillance.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that preparedness investments, aggressive contact containment, intensified mortality surveillance, research readiness, and digital coordination enabled rapid interruption of transmission in an urban SVD outbreak. They highlight the novelty of institutionalising mortality-led surveillance, domestic emergency financing, research readiness, and institutional quarantine of contacts as default policy for filovirus outbreaks in dense urban settings.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: They also underscore the value of coordinated resource allocation even with limited budgets for rapid outbreak control.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design, reliance on aggregated operational documents, and lack of primary patient-level data, which constrains causal inference and generalisability. analysis.summary_en: This study retrospectively analysed the 2025 Sudan virus disease (SVD) outbreak response in Kampala, Uganda, to identify innovations enabling rapid containment despite high urban transmission risk and constrained financing. Using a framework-based thematic analysis of operational documents, the authors found that 14 cases occurred across seven districts with a confirmed-case fatality rate of 16.7% and no deaths among treated patients. Key innovations included institutional quarantine of contacts, decentralised mobile laboratories, rapid deployment of therapeutics and vaccines via pre-approved research platforms, a real-time 4W coordination dashboard, and intensified mortality surveillance. The authors conclude that preparedness investments, aggressive contact containment, intensified mortality surveillance, research readiness, and digital coordination enabled rapid interruption of transmission. They recommend institutionalising mortality-led surveillance, domestic emergency financing, research readiness, and institutional quarantine of contacts as default policy for filovirus outbreaks in dense urban settings. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the retrospective design, reliance on aggregated documents, and absence of primary patient-level data.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 城市埃博拉苏丹病毒病 (SVD) 暴发 带来快速放大和跨区域传播的特殊风险,但 2025 年坎帕拉 暴发 尽管 传播 风险高且融资有限,但仍得到了遏制。该研究旨在确定能够实现快速控制的创新和系统调整,并为资源有限环境中的未来准备工作吸取经验教训。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 这项回顾性实施分析依据卫生部和世卫组织国家办事处的汇总业务文件,审查了乌干达 2025 年 SVD 暴发 的应对措施。暴发 于 2025 年 1 月 30 日在坎帕拉首次发现,涉及七个地区的 14 例病例。
elements_zh.methods: 使用世卫组织战略准备和应对计划支柱,将基于框架的主题分析应用于国家和地区应对计划、情况报告、实验室和 监测 摘要、行动后审查、政策和标准操作程序。没有从人类参与者那里收集主要数据,也没有访问可识别的个人患者数据。
elements_zh.main_results: 暴发 包括 14 例(12 例确诊,2 例疑似),确诊病例中有 2 例死亡(确诊病例死亡率 16.7%(2/12;95% CI 4.7–44.8)),埃博拉 治疗 病房收治的所有确诊病例均存活。主要创新包括对接触者进行机构隔离、分散的移动实验室、通过预先批准的研究平台快速部署治疗方法和 疫苗、实时 4W 协调仪表板以及强化的 死亡率 监测。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,准备投资、积极的接触遏制、强化的 死亡率 监测、研究准备和数字协调使得 传播 在城市 SVD 暴发 中迅速中断。他们强调了将 死亡率 主导的 监测 制度化、国内紧急融资、研究准备和接触者机构隔离作为密集城市环境中丝状病毒 暴发 的默认政策的新颖性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 他们还强调了协调资源分配的价值,即使预算有限,也能实现快速 暴发 控制。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其回顾性设计、对汇总操作文件的依赖以及缺乏主要患者数据而受到限制,从而限制了因果推断和普遍性。由于这些方法学限制和缺乏正式控制,证据强度被评估为中等。

analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,准备投资、积极的接触遏制、强化的 死亡率 监测、研究准备和数字协调使得 传播 在城市 SVD 暴发 中迅速中断。他们强调了将 死亡率 主导的 监测 制度化、国内紧急融资、研究准备和接触者机构隔离作为密集城市环境中丝状病毒 暴发 的默认政策的新颖性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 他们还强调了协调资源分配的价值,即使预算有限,也能实现快速 暴发 控制。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其回顾性设计、对汇总操作文件的依赖以及缺乏主要患者数据而受到限制,从而限制了因果推断和普遍性。由于这些方法学限制和缺乏正式控制,证据强度被评估为中等。

title_original: Emergence of a Bundibugyo virus variant in the 2026 outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed the emergence of a Bundibugyo virus variant during the 2026 outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda, highlighting a knowledge gap regarding the genomic and epidemiological characteristics of this variant and its implications for outbreak response.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study conducted a genomic and epidemiological investigation of the 2026 Bundibugyo virus outbreak, analyzing clinical samples and epidemiological data from affected regions in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda.
analysis.methods: Whole-genome sequencing was performed on clinical samples from confirmed cases, followed by phylogenetic and comparative genomic analyses to characterize the variant and trace its transmission dynamics. Epidemiological data were collected to assess outbreak spread and risk factors.
analysis.main_results: Genomic analysis identified a novel Bundibugyo virus variant with distinct mutations compared to historical strains, and phylogenetic reconstruction showed sustained human-to-human transmission within and between the two countries during the 2026 outbreak.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as evidence of a rapidly evolving Bundibugyo virus variant capable of sustained transmission, representing a novel public health challenge distinct from prior outbreaks. The study provides the first detailed genomic characterization of this variant in the context of a cross-border outbreak.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings underscore the need for enhanced genomic surveillance and rapid response strategies to detect and contain emerging Bundibugyo virus variants, particularly in regions with overlapping outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on a subset of available clinical samples and the absence of experimental validation of the variant's phenotypic properties, warranting cautious interpretation of the transmission dynamics and public health implications.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the emergence of a Bundibugyo virus variant during the 2026 outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda. Using whole-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis of clinical samples, researchers identified a novel variant with distinct mutations and evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission across borders. The authors interpret these findings as indicative of a rapidly evolving virus capable of sustained spread, representing a new public health challenge. The work highlights the importance of genomic surveillance and rapid response to detect and contain emerging variants, though limitations include reliance on a subset of samples and lack of experimental validation of phenotypic changes.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究讨论了 2026 年 暴发 期间在刚果民主共和国和乌干达出现的本迪布焦病毒变种,强调了有关该变种的基因组和流行病学特征及其对 暴发 应对的影响的知识差距。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究对2026年本迪布焦病毒暴发进行了基因组和流行病学调查,分析了刚果民主共和国和乌干达受影响地区的临床样本和流行病学数据。
elements_zh.methods: 对确诊病例的临床样本进行全 基因组 测序,然后进行系统发育和比较基因组分析,以表征变异并追踪其 传播 动态。收集流行病学数据以评估 暴发 的传播和危险因素。
elements_zh.main_results: 基因组分析发现了一种新的本迪布焦病毒变种,与历史毒株相比具有独特的 传播,系统发育重建显示 2026 年 暴发 期间两国内部和之间持续存在人与人之间的 传播。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为快速进化的本迪布焦病毒变种能够持续 传播 的证据,代表着与之前的 暴发 不同的新的公共卫生挑战。该研究首次在跨境 暴发 背景下详细描述了该变体的基因组特征。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果强调需要增强 基因组监测 和快速响应策略来检测和遏制新出现的本迪布焦病毒变种,特别是在 基因组监测 重叠的区域。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性在于其依赖于可用临床样本的子集,并且缺乏对该变体表型特性的实验验证,因此需要对 传播 动态和公共卫生影响进行谨慎解释。

analysis_zh.methods: 对确诊病例的临床样本进行全 基因组 测序,然后进行系统发育和比较基因组分析,以表征变异并追踪其 传播 动态。收集流行病学数据以评估 暴发 的传播和危险因素。
analysis_zh.main_results: 基因组分析发现了一种新的本迪布焦病毒变种,与历史毒株相比具有独特的 传播,系统发育重建显示 2026 年 暴发 期间两国内部和之间持续存在人与人之间的 传播。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为快速进化的本迪布焦病毒变种能够持续 传播 的证据,代表着与之前的 暴发 不同的新的公共卫生挑战。该研究首次在跨境 暴发 背景下详细描述了该变体的基因组特征。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果强调需要增强 基因组监测 和快速响应策略来检测和遏制新出现的本迪布焦病毒变种,特别是在 基因组监测 重叠的区域。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性在于其依赖于可用临床样本的子集,并且缺乏对该变体表型特性的实验验证,因此需要对 传播 动态和公共卫生影响进行谨慎解释。

full_text: On 4 September 2025, the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola virus disease in Kasai Province after laboratory testing at the National Institute of Biomedical Research in Kinshasa confirmed infection with Ebola virus, species Orthoebolavirus zairense [1]. At the time of declaration, 28 suspected cases and 15 deaths were reported, including four deaths among health-care workers, giving an early provisional case fatality ratio of approximately 54% [1]. The first known case was a 34-week pregnant woman admitted to Bulape General Reference Hospital on 20 August 2025 with fever, bloody diarrhoea, hemorrhage, vomiting, profound weakness, and subsequent multi-organ failure; she died on 25 August 2025 [1]. These early events highlighted the speed with which Ebola virus disease can move from an undifferentiated clinical syndrome to a high-consequence public health emergency, particularly when recognition occurs in peripheral health facilities with limited resources. Subsequent surveillance refined the epidemiological picture. By 30 November 2025, a total of 64 cases had been reported from six health areas in Bulape Health Zone, Kasai Province: 53 confirmed and 11 probable cases, with 45 deaths, corresponding to a reported case fatality ratio of 70.3% [2]. The outbreak was declared over on 1 December 2025 after 42 days had passed without new cases since the last confirmed patient tested negative and was discharged on 19 October 2025 [2, 3]. This final reporting is important because early outbreak figures are necessarily provisional and may change as case finding, laboratory confirmation, retrospective classification, and death investigations progress. The 2025 Kasai outbreak was the sixteenth Ebola virus disease outbreak reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was first identified in 1976 [2, 3]. Although the outbreak was ultimately contained within approximately three months, it resulted in substantial mortality and again demonstrated the vulnerability of remote health systems facing a highly lethal viral haemorrhagic fever. WHO initially assessed the public health risk as high at the national level, moderate at the regional level, and low at the global level [1]. This risk assessment remains an appropriate framing: the outbreak did not represent an imminent global spread scenario, but it did constitute a serious national and regional preparedness challenge with wider implications for global health security. Several features made the outbreak particularly concerning. Bulape Health Zone is a rural and difficult-to-access area, where transport, communication, laboratory referral, and clinical evacuation can be delayed [2, 4]. These operational constraints can slow case detection, isolation, safe referral, contact tracing, and safe and dignified burial practices. WHO reported that early transmission involved health-care-associated exposure and a high-transmission funeral event, both of which are well-recognized drivers of Ebola amplification [2]. Such patterns underline the importance of early clinical suspicion, immediate infection prevention and control measures, and community engagement from the first signs of a suspected cluster. Health-worker infections were among the most important signals of system vulnerability. Final WHO reporting documented five health-worker cases, including four nurses and one laboratory technician, three of whom died [2]. These infections should not be viewed only as occupational tragedies; they are also warning indicators of gaps in triage, personal protective equipment availability, infection prevention and control training, environmental hygiene, and early diagnostic pathways. In Ebola outbreaks, protecting health workers is central to protecting communities, because health facilities can either interrupt transmission or become sites of amplification. The response to the Kasai outbreak also illustrates how Ebola preparedness has evolved. The Ministry of Health, supported by WHO and partners, strengthened coordination, surveillance, laboratory diagnosis, case management, vaccination, infection prevention and control, safe burials, and risk communication [2, 3]. WHO deployed experts and frontline responders, delivered medical supplies and equipment, and supported mobile laboratory capacity to reduce diagnostic delays [2]. These measures cannot reverse the losses experienced by affected families and communities, but they likely contributed to interrupting transmission and limiting geographic spread. Vaccination was a major component of the response. Ebola vaccination began in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in September 2025 using the rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP vaccine, also known as Ervebo, initially targeting contacts, contacts of contacts, and frontline workers [5]. By the final outbreak report, 47,577 people had been vaccinated, including contacts, potential contacts, and at-risk individuals in affected areas [2]. The use of ring vaccination in Kasai was supported by evidence from previous Ebola responses, including the Guinea ring-vaccination trial, which demonstrated that rVSV-vectored vaccination could substantially reduce Ebola virus disease risk when deployed around confirmed cases and their contacts [6]. Further evidence from the Democratic Republic of the Congo has strengthened the case for rapid ring vaccination as part of an integrated outbreak-control strategy [7]. Therapeutic readiness has also improved compared with earlier Ebola outbreaks. During the Kasai response, patients received monoclonal antibody therapy as part of clinical management [2]. This reflects evidence from the PALM trial, which showed improved survival among patients treated with monoclonal antibody therapies compared with earlier investigational regimens [8]. WHO guidelines subsequently issued strong recommendations for monoclonal antibody therapies for Ebola virus disease caused by Ebola virus, when delivered alongside optimized supportive care [9]. Nevertheless, the high case fatality ratio in Kasai shows that the availability of therapeutics alone is insufficient. Survival depends on early presentation, rapid diagnosis, safe referral, adequate supportive care, timely treatment, and community trust in the response. The outbreak also reinforces the value of genomic surveillance. Whole-genome sequencing of early confirmed cases suggested that the 2025 Kasai outbreak was most likely caused by a new zoonotic spillover event rather than direct continuation of previous Kasai outbreaks [2]. This finding is scientifically important, but it should be interpreted with appropriate caution. Genomic inference depends on the completeness of sampling, the quality and timeliness of sequencing, and the availability of comparator genomes. Genomic data are most useful when integrated with field epidemiology, exposure histories, contact-tracing data, and ecological investigation. Community transmission risk in Ebola outbreaks is closely linked to direct contact with blood, body fluids, contaminated materials, and the bodies of people who have died from the disease [10]. Health-care exposure and burial-related exposure remain particularly important when infection prevention and control measures are not consistently implemented [10]. Therefore, community engagement is not an optional communication activity; it is a core technical intervention. Trusted local leaders, health workers, traditional healers, religious leaders, teachers, survivors, and community volunteers are essential for improving acceptance of surveillance, vaccination, safe care, safe burial practices, and survivor follow-up. The Kasai outbreak offers several practical lessons. First, decentralized surveillance and diagnostic capacity should be strengthened before outbreaks occur, especially in remote and historically affected regions. Second, infection prevention and control must be embedded into routine health-system practice rather than activated only after outbreak confirmation. Third, vaccine and therapeutic stockpiles must be matched by deployable cold-chain systems, trained teams, community trust, and clear operational protocols. Fourth, health-worker protection should be treated as a central outbreak-performance indicator. Finally, international financing for epidemic preparedness must be sustained. The successful containment of one outbreak should not create complacency, because the structural conditions that allow Ebola to emerge and spread often persist after the emergency declaration ends. This correspondence has limitations. It is based on publicly available outbreak reports and published literature, rather than patient-level surveillance or clinical datasets. It therefore cannot estimate transmission parameters, vaccine effectiveness, treatment effectiveness, time from symptom onset to isolation, or the independent impact of specific interventions. The reported fatality ratio may have been influenced by delayed detection, case ascertainment, health-seeking behavior, severity among detected cases, and classification of probable deaths. The available public data on health-worker infections are aggregated, limiting assessment of where and how occupational exposures occurred. Finally, although early genomic evidence suggested a likely zoonotic spillover event, the publicly available data are insufficient to fully reconstruct the source, exposure pathway, or complete transmission network. In conclusion, the 2025 Kasai Ebola outbreak was a serious but contained event. It caused substantial mortality, exposed persistent vulnerabilities in remote health systems, and again placed health workers at considerable risk. At the same time, it demonstrated the value of rapid coordination, mobile diagnostics, vaccination, clinical preparedness, risk communication, and international support. The declaration that an Ebola outbreak is over should mark the beginning of renewed preparedness, not the end of attention. Sustained investment in surveillance, infection prevention and control, genomic capacity, survivor follow-up, community trust, and health-system resilience remains essential to detect future outbreaks early, contain them rapidly, and protect both affected communities and the frontline workers who serve them. title_original: Ebola in Kasai, Democratic Republic of the Congo: Lessons from a Contained Outbreak for Epidemic Preparedness and Global Health Security

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed the persistent threat posed by Ebola virus disease (EVD) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where outbreaks recur despite prior experience, highlighting gaps in preparedness and response capacity. It examined why a contained 2025 outbreak in Kasai Province underscored the need for sustained epidemic preparedness and global health security measures.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This correspondence analyzed the 2025 EVD outbreak in Kasai Province, DRC, using publicly available outbreak reports and published literature rather than patient-level surveillance or clinical datasets. The outbreak was the sixteenth reported in the DRC since 1976 and was ultimately contained within approximately three months.
analysis.methods: Whole-genome sequencing of early confirmed cases was used to infer the outbreak's origin, while genomic inference relied on the completeness of sampling, sequencing quality, and availability of comparator genomes. The study synthesized evidence from WHO reports and published studies on ring vaccination and therapeutic trials.
analysis.main_results: By 30 November 2025, 64 cases were reported from six health areas in Bulape Health Zone, including 53 confirmed and 11 probable cases, with 45 deaths, yielding a reported case fatality ratio of 70.3%. Five health-worker cases were documented, with three deaths. Early transmission involved health-care-associated exposure and a high-transmission funeral event.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the outbreak as a serious but contained event that demonstrated the value of rapid coordination, mobile diagnostics, vaccination, clinical preparedness, risk communication, and international support. Novelty lies in synthesizing lessons from a recent outbreak to inform future preparedness strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings support strengthening decentralized surveillance and diagnostic capacity in remote regions, embedding infection prevention and control into routine health-system practice, and sustaining international financing for epidemic preparedness. They also emphasize the importance of community engagement in outbreak response.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited by its reliance on publicly available outbreak reports and published literature rather than patient-level data, precluding estimation of transmission parameters, vaccine effectiveness, or treatment impact. The study is assessed as moderate-strength due to potential biases in case ascertainment and reporting.

analysis.summary_en: The 2025 Ebola virus disease outbreak in Kasai Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, was the sixteenth reported in the country since 1976 and was ultimately contained within three months. By 30 November 2025, 64 cases (53 confirmed, 11 probable) and 45 deaths were reported, yielding a case fatality ratio of 70.3%, with five health-worker cases and three deaths. Early transmission involved health-care-associated exposure and a high-transmission funeral event. Whole-genome sequencing suggested a new zoonotic spillover rather than continuation of prior outbreaks. The response leveraged ring vaccination and improved therapeutic readiness, building on evidence from prior trials. The authors conclude that the outbreak highlighted the need for sustained epidemic preparedness, including decentralized surveillance, routine infection prevention and control, and international financing. However, the study's reliance on aggregated reports and literature limits precise estimation of transmission dynamics and intervention effectiveness.

title_zh: 刚果民主共和国开赛的埃博拉病毒:暴发 疫情防范和全球卫生安全的经验教训
source_body_en: This final reporting is important because early outbreak figures are necessarily provisional and may change as case finding, laboratory confirmation, retrospective classification, and death investigations progress. This finding is scientifically important, but it should be interpreted with appropriate caution. On 4 September 2025, the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola virus disease in Kasai Province after laboratory testing at the National Institute of Biomedical Research in Kinshasa confirmed infection with Ebola virus, species Orthoebolavirus zairense [1]. At the time of declaration, 28 suspected cases and 15 deaths were reported, including four deaths among health-care workers, giving an early provisional case fatality ratio of approximately 54% [1]. The first known case was a 34-week pregnant woman admitted to Bulape General Reference Hospital on 20 August 2025 with fever, bloody diarrhoea, hemorrhage, vomiting, profound weakness, and subsequent multi-organ failure; she died on 25 August 2025 [1]. These early events highlighted the speed with which Ebola virus disease can move from an undifferentiated clinical syndrome to a high-consequence public health emergency, particularly when recognition occurs in peripheral health facilities with limited resources. Subsequent surveillance refined the epidemiological picture. By 30 November 2025, a total of 64 cases had been reported from six health areas in Bulape Health Zone, Kasai Province: 53 confirmed and 11 probable cases, with 45 deaths, corresponding to a reported case fatality ratio of 70.3% [2].
